summary: Gives performance-related recommendations to users of network paths with very low bit-rate links. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: When the road is really narrow, here are tips for sending things so they get through quicker.

questions: tcp over very low bit rate links
how to speed up tcp on slow links
why disable tcp timestamps on slow links
subtitle: Practical advice for making TCP/IP feel faster over very low bit-rate links such as modems and wireless access.

tldr.problem: Slow last-hop links, such as 56 Kb/second modems or 4.8 Kb/second wireless, make interactive and bulky web traffic feel sluggish, and TCP can behave badly on them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo collects existing mechanisms: header and payload compression, small MTUs, active queue management in the last-hop router, sensible receive windows or auto-tuning, and Limited Transmit.
tldr.outcome: It is a pointer to existing IETF standards rather than a new protocol, and it recommends which to implement and which to avoid, such as TCP timestamps on these links.

facts.label: TCP/IP header overhead
facts.value: about 13 percent, down to 1-1.5 percent compressed

today: RFC 3150 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 48) and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It describes the Proposed Standard mechanisms of its time (July 2001), so the specific RFCs it cites may since have been replaced.

sections.title: The Slow Link Problem
sections.content:
The Internet protocol stack was designed to work across a wide range of link speeds. Older applications were either interactive but tiny (Telnet) or bulky but not interactive (FTP, network news). The World Wide Web produced traffic that is both interactive and often bulky: images, sound and video.

The Web also brought many users on slow last-hop links, and the memo expects more as mobile devices attach over slow wireless links. Its design space explicitly includes 56 Kb/second modem links and 4.8 Kb/second wireless access links.

To give good interactive response, implementors can send fewer bits by compressing the overhead and the payload. They can also tune TCP receive windows and queuing, which need no protocol changes. This document discusses general-purpose mechanisms and says where application-specific ones can do better.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people reach the Internet through a very thin pipe. This memo is about getting the most through it.

sections.title: Compressing Headers
sections.content:
TCP/IP header compression ( RFC 1144, RFC 2507, RFC 2508, RFC 2509, RFC 3095) improves interactive response and cuts overhead. For a typical dialup MTU of 296 bytes, header overhead falls from about 13 percent (typical 40-byte headers) to 1-1.5 percent (3-5 byte compressed headers). Shorter transmission times also expose packets to fewer loss events on lossy wireless links.

The schemes differ in how they cope with errors. RFC 1144 is widely deployed, but one bit error loses synchronization between compressor and decompressor. The result can be loss of up to a full TCP window, a full RTO of delay and an unnecessary slow-start. RFC 2507 can ask for retransmission of an uncompressed packet to resynchronize, which works much better on lossy links. For extreme cellular links (error conditions of 1e-3 or 1e-2 and round trip times over 100 ms), the Robust Header Compression group developed ROHC in RFC 3095.

The TCP timestamp option from RFC 1323 prevents header compression, because headers with changed TCP options are always sent uncompressed. The memo recommends against timestamps on slow links, which also do not need protection against sequence-number wrapping.

Recommendations: implement RFC 2507; PPP devices should implement RFC 2509; consider RFC 3095 for extremely slow, error-prone links if its complexity is justified; enable RFC 1144 only over reliable slow links.
sections.plainLanguage: Every parcel has a long address label. Squeezing the label down to a few letters leaves more room on a small truck for what is inside.

sections.title: Compressing Payloads
sections.content:
The IP Payload Compression Protocol (IPComp, RFC 2393) applies common compression algorithms to arbitrary IP payloads. The memo calls it a niche optimization. It is needed because IP-level security turns payloads into random-looking bits, which defeats link-layer compression.

Its benefit is limited because many payloads are already compressed (images, audio, video, zipped files) or encrypted above IP, as with SSL and TLS. HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616) already has Content-Encoding and Accept-Encoding for compressible types such as text/plain, leaving only the HTTP headers uncompressed. Application-level compression can often beat IPComp because it can use dictionaries based on the specific data.

Recommendation: IPComp may optionally be implemented. In HTTP/1.1 environments, payload compression should be implemented and used for payloads that are not already compressed.
sections.plainLanguage: Zipping a file makes it smaller before it goes down the thin pipe. A file that is already zipped cannot get much smaller.

sections.title: Choosing MTU Sizes
sections.content:
The memo gives several reasons to keep the MTU small on slow links:

  • If a full-length packet occupies the link longer than the delayed-ACK timeout (typically 200 milliseconds, up to 500), an ACK is sent for every segment instead of every second one.
  • Large packets create human-perceptible delays for other flows on the same link. RFC 1144 treats 100-200 millisecond delays as perceptible. The convention of a 296-byte MTU with header compression for dialup limits link occupancy to close to 200 milliseconds on 9.6 Kb/second links.
  • With a smaller MSS the congestion window grows faster when counted in segments, so there are more likely enough segments to produce three duplicate acknowledgements and trigger fast retransmit.
  • A smaller MTU also lowers queuing delay and so RTT.

There is one counterpoint: some networks charge per packet rather than per kilobyte, so a larger MTU can cost less there.

Recommendation: choose MTUs that do not monopolize the interface for human-perceptible time, and not significantly more than 100-200 milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: If one huge truck blocks the narrow road, everyone else has to wait. Smaller trucks let others slip through quickly.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Router Queues
sections.content:
A common setup is a laptop on dialup to a terminal server (the last-hop router), with an HTTP server on a fast LAN behind it. The server can send faster than the router can forward over the slow link, so the router becomes the point of congestion and drops packets. Slow start can overshoot the router buffer so several packets are lost in one window. The sender only learns about it one RTT later, and the congestion window can grow to double its size when the first drop happened.

Router buffer counts matter. Too few buffers (the memo cites only three per outbound link, as in RFC 2416) means even a small burst overflows. Many buffers with plain tail drop make queues long and RTT large, and can cause "lock-out", where a few connections occupy the queue. RFC 2309 recommends active queue management such as Random Early Detection (RED) in all routers, including last-hop routers, with RED parameters likely differing from the defaults. To absorb bursts from two or three senders with a typical burst of three back-to-back segments each, at least six or nine buffers are needed.

Hosts directly on a slow link may limit the receive window they advertise to avoid drops, but it must stay large enough to fill the link and to allow fast retransmit. Users should be able to choose the default receive window (even a simple dial-up/LAN choice), and applications should not try to manage bandwidth with socket buffer sizes. This advice fits hosts that always use slow links.
sections.plainLanguage: A fast road feeding a narrow road makes a traffic jam at the join. It helps to have a decent waiting area and to not let too many cars set off at once.

sections.title: Buffer Auto-tuning and Small Windows
sections.content:
Buffer auto-tuning allocates TCP buffers dynamically from the current congestion window instead of preallocating them. Receive buffers then suit the window in use, and send buffers hold two windows of segments so SACK and fast recovery can repair losses without long retransmission timeouts. For a host that sometimes uses a slow link and sometimes much faster ones, the memo says it may use receive buffer auto-tuning to set an appropriate advertised window.

On a slow link the congestion window may settle at only a few segments, too few to produce three duplicate acknowledgements. A retransmission timeout is then needed and the window drops to one segment. Limited Transmit (RFC 3042) sends a new segment on the first and second duplicate ACKs so the receiver can keep producing duplicates until fast retransmit triggers. At most two extra new segments are sent this way, and they are ACK-clocked, not back-to-back.

Recommendation: Limited Transmit should be implemented in all hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: With very few packets in flight, the sender cannot tell a lost one from a slow one. Sending one extra packet gives it clues sooner.

sections.title: Summary of Recommendations
sections.content:
The memo's summary says that all the mechanisms listed are stable standards-track RFCs at Proposed Standard status as of writing. Buffer auto-tuning is not a standards-track mechanism but an operating system implementation issue.

  • Header compression should be implemented. RFC 1144 over robust links, RFC 2507 where corruption loss is expected, and ROHC evaluated for extremely lossy and slow links.
  • RFC 1323 TCP timestamps must be turned off on these links.
  • IPComp should be implemented, and HTTP/1.1 payload compression used for payloads not already compressed.
  • MTUs should not hold the interface for more than 100-200 milliseconds.
  • Active queue management is recommended on last-hop routers, with enough buffers for concurrent bursts.
  • Default TCP receive windows should account for hosts on low-speed links.
  • Limited Transmit should be implemented in all end hosts.

Header compression is the only item that may stop working under end-to-end IPsec, though ROHC can compress the ESP header.
sections.plainLanguage: The short version: shrink the labels, shrink the contents if you can, use small trucks, manage the waiting area, and send one extra clue packet when things look lost.

sections.title: Further Work and Security Notes
sections.content:
For further work the memo mentions more compact HTTP headers. It calls the HTTP-NG proposal defunct and says HTTP/1.1 is not being enhanced with a compact header form, while the WAP Forum chose the Wireless Session Protocol with its own compact header encoding. It also notes that TCP options that change between segments, like timestamps and selective acknowledgements, disable today's header compression, and that the Robust Header Compression group is working on this. Delta encoding of HTTP resources is another effort to follow.

On security, the memo proposes no protocol changes. Apart from Van Jacobson compression (RFC 1144) and RFC 2507, 2508 and 2509, the mechanisms work with TCP protected by end-to-end IPsec. ROHC works only partly, since encryption makes any payload data and subsequent headers uncompressible. There are no IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: People are still looking for ways to shrink web messages more. Encrypted messages cannot be squeezed much, which is why some tricks stop working with them.
